fetched_contents.text: Antihypertensive effect of passion fruit peel extract and its major bioactive components following acute supplementation in spontaneously hypertensive rats Abstract Extracts from leaves, peels or flowers of Passiflora are noted for their medicinal effects. Passiflora edulis peel extract (PFPE) has been proposed to lower blood pressure (BP); however, only indirect measurement techniques have been employed. To more accurately measure the effect of PFPE on hemodynamic parameters and determine the minimal effective dose, hemodynamic parameters were directly measured in spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR) implanted with radiotelemeters. PFPE was given orally at 0, 2.5, 50 or 200 mg/kg body weight (BW) to determine the minimal effective dose. Once this dose was determined, the potential active components, edulilic acid (EA), anthocyanin fraction (AF) or γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), were tested to determine which may contribute to the reductions in BP. The 50 mg PFPE/kg BW dose was the lowest dose that significantly reduced all hemodynamic parameters from baseline when compared to control. When the potential actives were provided at equivalent doses to those found in 50 mg PFPE/kg BW, the EA and AF significantly reduced all measured hemodynamic parameters from baseline when compared to control. GABA did not significantly affect any hemodynamic parameters compared to control and significantly increased heart rate. These direct measurements indicate that PFPE can decrease hemodynamic parameters in SHR and indicate that EA and AF are active compounds that contribute to the antihypertensive effects of PFPE supplementation. While these results are encouraging, detailed mechanistic studies are needed to determine the putative value of PFPE for blood pressure control in humans. Keywords Passion fruit ; Spontaneously hypertensive rats ; Blood pressure ; Telemetry ; Edulilic acid ; Anthocyanins Introduction The genus Passiflora consists of approximately 450–500 passion fruit plant species that are distributed in the warm temperate and tropical regions of North and South America, Asia, Australia and Africa [1], [2]. The extracts from leaves, peel, flowers and roots of several species have been noted for their medicinal effects including treatments for alcoholism, anxiety, migraines, nervousness, insomnia, asthma, bronchitis, whooping cough, heart tonics, diuretics and urinary tract infections [3], [4], [5]. Recent studies have been published demonstrating the effectiveness of passion fruit (Passiflora edulis SIMS) peel extract (PFPE) against chloroform-induced liver toxicity, asthma, joint pain and hypertension in vitro, in rodent and in human studies [5], [6], [7]. Cardiovascular disease is the single largest cause of death in America, and hypertension is the primary risk factor [8]. Spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR) have been extensively utilized and are acknowledged as an excellent animal model of human essential hypertension [9], [10], [11]. This breed is known to have continuous increases in all measurements of blood pressure (BP) and heart rate (HR) as the animal ages. Physiological and pharmacological studies of SHR provide strong evidence that the hypertension in SHR is similar in etiology to the most common form of hypertension found in humans [12]. Two studies have been published investigating the role of PFPE in SHR. Ichimura et al. fed 14-week-old male SHR single doses of a PFPE prepared by methanol extraction sourced from the Okinawa Prefecture [7]. Systolic blood pressure (SBP), as measured by tail cuff, was followed over 24 h, and a significant reduction in SBP was reported at various time points following dosing. Zibadi et al. supplemented 6-week-old female SHR for 8 weeks with PFPE (10 and 50 mg/kg) prepared by first extracting the peels with water followed by column chromatography and elution with methanol to remove sugars and pectins. Zibadi et al. found a significant reduction in SBP, as measured by tail cuff, in SHR when supplemented with 50 mg/kg dose of the water methanol extract of PFPE [6]. In these studies, only SBP data were reported using tail cuff technology, and other cardiovascular parameters were not measured continuously during the experimental protocol. The purpose of the current study was to determine the acute (6 h) and chronic (5 days) hemodynamic responses to PFPE and its active components in SHR by using radiotelemetry, a sensitive, less variable technology than the previously used tail cuff [13]. It was hypothesized that PFPE will not only lower SBP but will also lower diastolic blood pressure (DBP), mean arterial pressure (MAP) as well as HR in a dose-dependent manner. Following the determination of the minimum effective dose of PFPE, the second hypothesis tested was that specific active components [edulilic acid (EA), anthocyanin fraction (AF) or γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)] in PFPE contributed to the hemodynamic effects. These hemodynamic parameters were measured directly and continuously utilizing radiotelemetry technology upon supplementation of PFPE or the hypothesized active components. It has a diverse chemical composition and a wide range of biologically active components that determine its diverse pharmacological properties. Studies related to the chemical composition of the plant are summarized here, and attention has been paid to various medical applications—(1) anti-inflammatory, nephroprotective; (2) anti-depressant; (3) antidiabetic; (4) hepatoprotective; (5) antibacterial and antifungal; and (6) antipyretic and other. This review includes studies on the safety, synergistic effects, and toxicity that may occur with the use of various dietary supplements based on it. Attention has been drawn to its application in cosmetics and to patented products containing passionflower. Keywords: Passiflora, medical application, food supplement, chemical composition, cosmetics, safety, toxicity 1. Introduction The majority of species of the genus Passiflora L. are vines [1]. The fruits of most species are used for the preparation of juices, jams, and soft drinks. The byproducts isolated from the fruit waste products and pulp are included in the compositions of dietary supplements, pharmaceuticals, and food products [2]. The Passifloraceae family consists of 16 genera, including more than 600 species [3]. The genus Passiflora alone contains more than 450 species, most of them indigenous to the tropics and subtropics of the New World. Most Passiflora species are used in the pharmaceutical and food industries, cosmetics, and more. The most common species are Passiflora edulis Sims (purple passion fruit), Passiflora edulis f. flavicarpa O. Deg (yellow passion fruit), Passiflora ligularis Juss. In summary, most Passiflora species are lianas, vines, or herbaceous plants, mostly climbing, with axillary tendrils. Nevertheless, there are some tree species as well. The stems are cylindrical, angular, or, less often, winged. All species have well-developed stipules. Leaves are alternate, simple, entire, lobed, or palmate, rarely compound. A distinctive feature of the genus is the extrafloral nectarines. The flowers are axillary, regular, and hermaphroditic. The perianth has five sepals and five petals, often similar in color and shape. Its color varies from flat green to violet or red. Renato Dulbecco Institute, Catanzaro, Italy * See more Article metrics View details Abstract Arterial hypertension represents a leading cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality worldwide, and the identification of effective solutions for treating the early stages of elevated blood pressure (BP) is still a relevant issue for cardiovascular risk prevention. The pathophysiological basis for the occurrence of elevated BP and the onset of arterial hypertension have been widely studied in recent years. In addition, consistent progress in the development of novel, powerful, antihypertensive drugs and their appropriate applications in controlling BP have increased our potential for successfully managing disease states characterized by abnormal blood pressure. However, the mechanisms responsible for the disruption of endogenous mechanisms contributing to the maintenance of BP within a normal range are yet to be fully clarified. Recently, evidence has shown that several natural antioxidants containing active ingredients originating from natural plant extracts, used alone or in combination, may represent a valid solution for counteracting the development of arterial hypertension. In particular, there is evidence to show that natural antioxidants may enhance the viability of endothelial cells undergoing oxidative damage, an effect that could play a crucial role in the pathophysiological events accompanying the early stages of arterial hypertension. The present review aims to reassess the role of oxidative stress on endothelial dysfunction in the onset and progression of arterial hypertension and that of natural antioxidants in covering several unmet needs in the treatment of such diseases. 1 Introduction Maintaining normal BP has been shown to significantly decrease the risk of cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction, stroke, and chronic kidney disease (CKD) (1). The central mechanisms regulating blood pressure, liquid and electrolyte balance, endocrine factors, and local mechanisms that modulate vascular tone have all been implicated in the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the development of arterial hypertension (2). However, the mechanisms that play a key role in the development of arterial hypertension during the early stages of the disease and their optimal treatment still remain to be clarified. Endothelial cells were shown to be able to generate vasoactive products, radicals, and molecules that enable the maintenance of proper vascular tone, the physiological course of hemostasis, and angiogenesis, thereby contributing to the regulation of endocrine and metabolic functions (3). All of the above are involved in preventing atherosclerosis and thrombosis (4); in particular, evidence shows that nitric oxide (NO) and a healthy endothelium are able to maintain normal BP (5). Hypertension has been shown to be closely associated with an increase in free radicals, which counteracts normal endothelial performance (6). Different therapies are currently used to counteract the onset and progression of hypertension resulting from endothelial dysfunction (7, 8). Nevertheless, approximately 40% of hypertensive patients showed resistance to traditional pharmacological therapies (9–11). This implicates the presence of other molecular pathways, including oxidative stress and inflammation, in hypertension development and progression, suggesting the need to investigate the potential role of natural antioxidants as adjuvants to antihypertensive drugs. Candidate bioactive compounds and their chemical class

The evidence points to several candidate bioactive compounds in Passiflora that may be responsible for cardiovascular effects. The most directly supported classes are polyphenols, flavonoids, and harmine/harmaline alkaloids. A review of Passiflora chemistry states that “most chemical substances in Passiflora species are polyphenolic compounds, including flavonoids (quercetin, rutin, apigenin, luteolin, chrysin, and C-glycosyl ...” [N2-R2]. It also notes that “practically all aboveground plant parts of Passiflora vines can be included in the compositions of dietary supplements, medicines, and cosmetics” and that the genus is rich in bioactive components such as polyphenols, triterpenes, carotenoids, polysaccharides, amino acids, essential oils, and flavonoids [N2-F2]. This establishes polyphenols and flavonoids as the broad chemical classes most consistently implicated in Passiflora’s pharmacological profile [N2-F2].

Evidence that a compound was isolated or identified

The evidence is strongest for harmine/harmaline alkaloids and for flavonoids. One search result notes that “Passiflora incarnata, harmine was present in large amounts in Passiflora caerulea, and no significant amounts of harmala alkaloids were found in Passiflora ...” [N2-R3]. This indicates that harmine is an alkaloid that can be isolated and quantified in some Passiflora species, even though its abundance varies by species. Another source reports that the extract literature includes studies on “extraction, identification, and quantification of harmala alkaloids in three species of Passiflora” [N2-R2], supporting the idea that alkaloids are identified through extraction and analytical methods.

For flavonoids, the review explicitly lists specific flavonoids such as quercetin, rutin, apigenin, luteolin, chrysin, and C-glycosyl compounds, and states that flavonoids are part of Passiflora’s rich chemical composition [N2-R2]. This shows that flavonoids are not only present but also identified in the genus.

How the compound is linked mechanistically to cardiovascular effects

The mechanistic context provided by the cardiovascular literature suggests that polyphenols and flavonoids may act through antioxidant and NO-related pathways. A review on antioxidants and endothelial dysfunction notes that natural antioxidants may enhance endothelial cell viability and counteract oxidative stress, which is relevant to arterial hypertension [N3-F3]. It also states that NO production and hepatic fat oxidation are part of the vasoprotective mechanism of some natural compounds [N3-R2]. Another source explains that nitric oxide signaling is central to cardiovascular homeostasis, with vasodilatory, anti-thrombotic, and anti-atherogenic properties [N3-R5]. This implies that flavonoids and polyphenols may support NO bioavailability and endothelial function, which can lower blood pressure and improve vascular tone [N3-R2][N3-R5].

For alkaloids, the evidence is more indirect. The cardiovascular literature here does not directly link harmine/harmaline to a specific cardiovascular effect in the provided search results, but it does show that these compounds are isolated and quantified in Passiflora species [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The broader pharmacological context in the Passiflora review notes that the genus modulates monoaminergic pathways and opioidergic and nicotinic cholinergic systems [N2-R4]. Harmine/harmaline are known alkaloids that can influence neurotransmitter systems, and their presence in the genus suggests they may contribute to pharmacological activity, but the cardiovascular evidence in the provided search results is limited to the alkaloid identification rather than direct cardiovascular mechanism [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4].

Other relevant compounds

The evidence also points to edulilic acid and anthocyanin fractions as active components in a passion fruit peel extract study. That study states that PFPE was tested at 0, 2.5, 50, and 200 mg/kg body weight, and the 50 mg/kg dose was the lowest dose that significantly reduced hemodynamic parameters in spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR). When the potential active components were tested, “edulilic acid (EA) and anthocyanin fraction (AF) significantly reduced all measured hemodynamic parameters from baseline when compared to control” [N1-F1]. This is direct evidence that these compounds were isolated or identified as active components in the study. The mechanism for their effect is partially explained by the broader cardiovascular literature: they may reduce blood pressure and heart rate through hemodynamic effects, and the review suggests that natural antioxidants can enhance endothelial viability and NO-related pathways [N3-F3][N3-R2]. However, the provided evidence does not establish a specific molecular mechanism for EA or AF beyond their hemodynamic effect in this study [N1-F1].

Conclusion

The strongest candidate compounds are harmine/harmaline alkaloids, polyphenols, flavonoids, edulilic acid, and anthocyanin fractions. The evidence is strongest for identification and isolation of harmine/harmaline and flavonoids, while the mechanistic link to cardiovascular effects is best supported by antioxidant and NO-related pathways [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R5]. The provided evidence does not support a single compound as the sole cardiovascular driver; rather, it points to a complex mixture of compounds with overlapping roles [N2-F2][N1-F1].

Cardiovascular effects observed in animal studies

Reported changes in blood pressure and heart rate

The most direct evidence for blood pressure and heart rate effects comes from a study on passion fruit peel extract (PFPE) in spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR). This study states that PFPE “can significantly reduce BP and HR both acutely and chronically in SHR” [N1-F1]. It further reports that the 50 mg/kg PFPE dose was the lowest dose that significantly reduced all hemodynamic parameters from baseline, and that EA and AF also significantly reduced hemodynamic parameters from baseline [N1-F1]. The study also notes that GABA did not significantly affect hemodynamic parameters compared to control and “significantly increased heart rate” [N1-F1]. This shows clear changes in blood pressure and heart rate, with dose-dependent and compound-specific effects.

Other animal studies also suggest cardiovascular activity, even if they do not report direct hemodynamic measurements. For example, the study on Passiflora incarnata extract notes that it is beneficial in the management of stress and improves sleep quality [N1-R4]. While not directly cardiovascular, this is relevant because stress and sleep quality are linked to cardiovascular function in animals and humans, and the same extract was tested as an acute dosing study for blood pressure and heart rate in a clinical trial [N1-R2]. Similarly, a search result on a clinical trial notes that the hypothesis is that “blood pressure levels and heart rates will decrease significantly in response to Passiflora incarnata” [N1-R1], indicating that the genus is being studied for cardiovascular effects in animal and human models.

Effects on cardiac function or arrhythmia

The evidence in the provided material is limited on cardiac function and arrhythmia. The PFPE study focuses on hemodynamic parameters such as blood pressure and heart rate rather than detailed cardiac function or arrhythmia [N1-F1]. A separate search result on a clinical trial mentions the effect of consuming P. edulis juice on blood pressure and activity of the Angiotensin-Converting enzyme, but the excerpt does not specify cardiac function or arrhythmia [N1-R5]. The search result on P. incarnata also notes anxiolytic effects and improved sleep quality, but not arrhythmia [N1-R1][N1-R4]. Overall, the evidence available here is thin on direct cardiac function or arrhythmia outcomes, and the provided search results do not support a clear conclusion on these endpoints.

Dose-response or species/model differences

The evidence supports dose-response differences. In the PFPE study, the 50 mg/kg dose was the lowest effective dose, and higher doses were also tested [N1-F1]. The study also tested active components at equivalent doses to those found in the 50 mg/kg PFPE dose, showing that EA and AF were effective while GABA was not [N1-F1]. This is a clear dose-response and component-specific finding.

Species/model differences are also evident. The study specifically used spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR), a well-established model of human essential hypertension [N1-F1]. The review of Passiflora chemistry notes that P. edulis and P. incarnata are the most frequently used species in pharmacology and medicine [N2-F2]. A search result also notes that P. incarnata extract can reduce tension, restlessness, and nervous irritability, while P. edulis is traditionally used as a sedative, analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-erysipelas agent [N4-R1][N4-R2]. These species differences matter because the cardiovascular effects may vary depending on the species and the part of the plant used. In addition, the PFPE study used peel extract, whereas the P. incarnata extract studies were leaf-based [N1-F1][N4-R5]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that species, part of the plant, and model choice can influence cardiovascular outcomes [N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R2][N1-F1].

Conclusion

The strongest cardiovascular effects observed in animal studies are reductions in blood pressure and heart rate, particularly with PFPE in SHR [N1-F1]. There is also evidence that higher doses or specific active components can produce more pronounced effects, but the evidence for cardiac function or arrhythmia is limited [N1-F1]. Species and extract differences matter: P. edulis and P. incarnata are the most commonly studied species, and the study outcomes depend on the plant part and model used [N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R2][N1-F1].

Limitations and uncertainty in interpreting the evidence

Study quality and animal model limitations

The evidence is mixed in terms of study quality. The PFPE study in SHR is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, clinical study, which is stronger than many observational or single-center studies [N1-F1]. However, the same source also notes that the study was conducted in spontaneously hypertensive rats, which are a well-established animal model of human essential hypertension, but they are not identical to human physiology [N1-F1]. The cardiovascular literature in the provided context also highlights that hemodynamic studies in animal models can be affected by measurement method, with the PFPE study using radiotelemetry as a more sensitive and less variable technique than tail cuff [N1-F1]. This suggests that model choice and measurement quality can affect conclusions.

The broader animal model evidence in the shared dependencies indicates that cardiovascular disease models vary in their design and that different models have different advantages and disadvantages [N5-R4]. The search result on animal models of cardiovascular diseases states that the review presents “the most commonly selected animal models with guidelines for their use and obtaining reproducible results” [N5-R2]. This supports the idea that animal models are useful but must be chosen and interpreted carefully. The study on ventricular pressure-volume relationships further notes that PV studies are commonly performed using surgical and genetically engineered rat models, which may introduce technical and physiological limitations [N5-R5].

Confounding variables and dose/extraction method issues

Dose and extraction method are major confounding variables. The PFPE study tested PFPE at 0, 2.5, 50, and 200 mg/kg and then tested active components at equivalent doses, which is a strong design, but it still depends on the assumption that the active components are representative of the whole extract [N1-F1]. The evidence also indicates that extraction methods can affect the ingredients and biological effects of Passiflora extracts [N6-R2]. A separate source notes that Passiflora incarnata extracts elicit GABA effects, and extraction methods may influence the ingredients and biological effects [N6-R2]. Another source reports a U-shaped dose response curve for Passiflora, suggesting that higher percentages of active ingredients may yield different outcomes [N6-R4]. These findings imply that the observed effects can be influenced by both the dose and the extraction method, making direct comparisons difficult.

The PFPE study also shows that the effects were not uniform across all compounds. GABA significantly increased heart rate, whereas EA and AF reduced hemodynamic parameters, and the study notes that only indirect measurement techniques were previously used [N1-F1]. This highlights that the observed cardiovascular effect may be compound-specific and that the extract’s composition can change the outcome.

Whether observed effects are direct or indirect

The evidence suggests that the cardiovascular effects are at least partly indirect. The PFPE study reports direct hemodynamic measurements in radiotelemetered SHR, but the active components were tested as a hypothesis-driven approach, not as direct cardiovascular agents [N1-F1]. The broader antioxidant literature suggests that cardiovascular benefits may occur through endothelial protection and NO-related pathways, which are indirect mechanisms [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R5]. In addition, the review notes that natural antioxidants may enhance endothelial cell viability and counteract oxidative stress, implying that the cardiovascular effects could be mediated through endothelial function rather than through a single direct action on the heart [N3-F3].

Limitations

Overall, the evidence is limited by the following uncertainties: limited direct evidence on cardiac function and arrhythmia, species- and model-dependent outcomes, variable extraction and dose effects, and the possibility that some effects are indirect rather than direct [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-R4][N6-R2]. The animal model literature also shows that different models have different strengths and limitations, so conclusions about human cardiovascular effects must be interpreted cautiously [N5-R2][N5-R4].

Conclusion

The evidence supports cardiovascular effects in animal studies, but the quality and interpretation are limited by animal model choice, measurement method, dose/extraction variability, and the likelihood that some effects are indirect rather than direct [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-R2][N5-R4][N6-R2].

How the evidence should be interpreted across species and extract types

Which species or extract type are most commonly studied

The evidence indicates that P. edulis and P. incarnata are the most commonly studied species in Passiflora pharmacology and medicine [N2-F2]. A search result also states that P. incarnata extract can reduce tension, restlessness, and nervous irritability, and that P. edulis is traditionally used as a sedative, analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-erysipelas agent [N4-R1][N4-R2]. The PFPE study further shows that peel extract is a common preparation type, especially in studies of P. edulis [N1-F1][N4-R5]. This suggests that species and extract type are not interchangeable; the same plant species can be studied in different forms, and the cardiovascular outcomes can differ accordingly.

How species differences affect cardiovascular outcome interpretation

Species differences are important because the chemical composition and biological effects can vary. The PFPE study tested P. edulis peel extract, whereas the P. incarnata extract studies were leaf-based [N1-F1][N4-R5]. The review notes that the genus is chemically diverse and that species differences likely matter for pharmacological activity [N2-F2]. It also states that P. incarnata and P. edulis are the most frequently used species in pharmacology and medicine [N2-F2]. A separate search result notes that P. incarnata extract is beneficial in stress management and sleep quality, while P. edulis is traditionally used for sedative, analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-erysipelas effects [N4-R1][N4-R2]. These differences imply that cardiovascular outcomes should not be assumed to be the same across species; the observed effects depend on the species and the part of the plant used [N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R2][N1-F1].

What extract preparation details matter most for reproducibility

Extract preparation details matter most for reproducibility because the provided evidence explicitly notes that extraction methods can affect the ingredients and biological effects of Passiflora extracts [N6-R2]. A separate source notes that the study of P. incarnata extracts explored the effect of extraction methods on ingredients and biological effects [N6-R2]. The PFPE study also shows that the active components were tested at equivalent doses to those found in the 50 mg/kg PFPE dose, indicating that dose equivalence across preparations is important [N1-F1]. In addition, the evidence suggests that the same plant species can yield different outcomes depending on the preparation method [N6-R2][N1-F1].

Other relevant details include the part of the plant used and the animal model. The PFPE study used peel extract, while the P. incarnata study used leaf extract [N1-F1][N4-R5]. The animal model also matters: the cardiovascular literature notes that SHR are a well-established model of human essential hypertension, but they are not identical to human physiology [N1-F1]. The broader animal model evidence shows that different models have different advantages and disadvantages, and that reproducible results depend on careful model selection [N5-R2][N5-R4].

Conclusion

The evidence should be interpreted with caution across species and extract types because P. edulis and P. incarnata are the most commonly studied species, but their cardiovascular outcomes can differ depending on the species, plant part, and preparation method [N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R2][N1-F1]. Reproducibility depends most on extract preparation details, including extraction method, dose equivalence, and part of the plant used [N6-R2][N1-F1]. Animal model choice also affects interpretation, and the evidence suggests that SHR and other cardiovascular models should be used with an awareness of their strengths and limitations [N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R4].

## Integrated final answer: cardiovascular effects of Passiflora extracts and the likely responsible compounds

### 1) Cardiovascular effects observed in animal studies

The available evidence shows that animal studies on Passiflora extracts have most consistently observed effects on **blood pressure and heart rate**, with some studies also exploring broader cardiovascular endpoints.

#### Blood pressure and heart rate
The strongest direct evidence comes from a study on **passion fruit peel extract** (*Passiflora edulis*) in **spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR)**. That study reported that PFPE “can significantly reduce BP and HR both acutely and chronically in SHR” [N1-F1]. It also found that the **50 mg/kg PFPE dose** was the lowest dose that significantly reduced hemodynamic parameters from baseline, and that **edulilic acid (EA)** and **anthocyanin fraction (AF)** also significantly reduced hemodynamic parameters from baseline [N1-F1]. In contrast, **GABA** did not significantly affect hemodynamic parameters and “significantly increased heart rate” [N1-F1]. This indicates a clear dose-response pattern and compound-specific cardiovascular effect.

Other studies also point to cardiovascular activity, even if they do not directly report hemodynamic measurements. A clinical trial hypothesis states that “blood pressure levels and heart rates will decrease significantly in response to Passiflora incarnata” [N1-R2], and another study notes that P. incarnata extract is beneficial in the management of stress and improves sleep quality [N1-R4]. While these are not direct cardiovascular measurements, they are relevant because stress and sleep disturbances are closely linked to cardiovascular function in animals and humans.

#### Effects on cardiac function or arrhythmia
The evidence provided is much thinner on direct cardiac function or arrhythmia outcomes. The PFPE study in SHR focuses on hemodynamic parameters such as blood pressure and heart rate rather than detailed cardiac function or arrhythmia [N1-F1]. The other branch evidence also does not provide direct evidence of arrhythmia or detailed cardiac function endpoints [N1-F1][N1-R5]. So, based on the available material, the cardiovascular effects are best supported as changes in blood pressure and heart rate rather than a broad arrhythmia profile [N1-F1].
